p.seg: Yet since the two capitals fell into enemy hands,
and the four barbarian tribes claimed sovereignty,
with barbarians and Chinese intermingling,
their language and expressions became especially crude.
As for Yànluán and Bóqǐ,
they were intent on preserving concealments and taboos;
old annotations
called "long"
as "cáng",
likely to avoid using Emperor Yáo Cháng's personal name.
Chóngguī and Délín,
aimed at literary embellishment.
Thus for several hundred years within the Central Kingdom,
its customs cannot be properly discussed.
As the saying goes:
"To know antiquity but not the present
is called being submerged on land."
O scribes who wield the brush,
how cautious you must be!
Furthermore, the conciseness in narration
flows in two streams:
one is the omission of sentences,
the other is the omission of words.
For instance, in the *Zuǒ Zhuàn*, when Huà Ǒu of Sòng came to form an alliance,
he mentioned that his ancestor had offended Sòng,
and the people of Lǔ considered him quick-witted.
Now, to call a dull person quick-witted—the people of Lǔ referred to a dull person. The *Lǐjì* already contains an annotation.,
thus it is clear that the wise and enlightened would ridicule this,
which is an example of omitting sentences.
The *Chūnqiū Jīng* states:
"Five meteorites fell in Sòng."
Now, hearing that they fell,
seeing that they were stones,
and counting them as five.
Adding one word would be too detailed,
subtracting one word would be too brief;
seeking a balance between them,
it is concise and reasonable,
which is an example of omitting words.
There are cases contrary to this,
such as in the *Gǔliáng Zhuàn*, which states that Xì Kè was blind in one eye,
Jìsūn Xíngfú was bald,
Sūn Liángfū was lame,
and the envoy of Qí had a lame man welcome the lame man,
a bald man welcome the bald man,
a one-eyed man welcome the one-eyed man,
a hunchback welcome the hunchback.
It would be appropriate to remove the phrases starting with "lame man"
and below,
and simply say, "Each welcomed according to their kind."
If everything must be repeated,
then the text becomes excessively verbose,
which is an example of redundant sentences.
The *Hànshū•Zhāng Cāng Zhuàn* states:
"He was old in years,
and had no teeth in his mouth."
Here, within this single sentence, the words "in years"
and "in his mouth"
could be omitted.
Thus, this sentence of six characters
has three characters unnecessarily added,
which is an example of redundant words.
However, omitting sentences is easier,
while omitting words is more difficult.
Only with deep insight into this principle
can one begin to discuss historiography.
If sentences are filled with superfluous content,
and words are all repetitive,
the verbosity and clutter in historical writing
are primarily due to this.
In Bān Gù's compiled treatises,
there are many inconsistencies.
Regarding the "Treatise on the Five Elements,"
the redundancies are particularly severe.
Now I shall enumerate their errors,
categorizing them into four types:
first, improper citation of texts;
second, narratives contrary to reason;
third, excessive interpretation of calamities;
fourth, lack of mastery in classical learning.
Furthermore, within these four categories,
I will delineate various subitems,
one is written as "treatise," which is incorrect.
Grouping and distinguishing them by category.
One version reads "distinguishing."
They are compiled as follows.
Observing the book of Zuǒshì,
it stands as the foremost commentary,
yet through the Han and Wei dynasties,
it ultimately was not included in the official curriculum.
Confucian scholars all dismissed this single school,
and fervently promoted the two other commentaries.
Considering that Qiūmíng personally served as a historian of Lǔ,
and received the classics from Zhòngní,
in terms of era they were contemporaries,
in terms of talent they shared the same sensibilities.
One version reads "substance," which is incorrect.
Those two schools,
were taught by disciples of Master Kǒng,
and followers of later learned men,
their talent and understanding were fundamentally different,
and separated by generations—
how could one hold their transmitted explanations
to compare with this direct transmission!
Moreover, the two commentaries contain unreasonable and biased principles,
their words are often crude and unrefined—
when compared to Zuǒshì,
they cannot be mentioned in the same breath.
Thus we know that the Gāohuāng and Mòshǒu
are but the baseless accounts of pedantic scholars;
the Màibǐng and Tàiguān,
truly reflect the discerning judgment of wise men.
To undertake affairs without following antiquity,
is something I have never heard of in the teachings of Fù Shuō;
if one models oneself on the sages of the past,
the principle should not be concealed.
Yet when Wèi Shōu established his rules,
he entirely adopted those of Fàn Yèzōng,
coveting the achievements of heaven as his own merit—
unlike Fàn Yè, who followed Shū Jùn,
or Bān Gù, who learned from Zǐcháng.
How could he roll up his sleeves and act openly,
without falling into the crime of tunneling through walls?
It is also said:
"A gentleman is ashamed if there is one thing he does not know."
Thus, whether the time be remote or recent,
whether the matter be great or small,
one must rely on
extensive learning to achieve broad knowledge.
As for today's
so-called expressions,
such as calling "Hàn" in the Central Plains,
"Qiāng" in the area west of Hángu Pass,
using "nú" for minister,
and addressing mother as "zǐ".
The sovereign has the title of "dàjiā",
and people refer to masters with the term "érláng".
These six phrases all refer to currently popular colloquial expressions.
There are many examples of this kind,
too numerous to count.
One must trace their origins,
though their sources are often unclear.
Upon reading the Qí Records,
written by Wáng Shào,
they become clear and understandable.
From this perspective,
what Shào recorded
provides immense benefit.
It is sufficient to enlighten the obscured minds of later scholars,
and broaden the understanding of future generations.
Without Jūnmào (Wáng Shào's courtesy name),
I would have been ignorant of recent matters like one facing a wall.
How could you rashly mock and ridicule him!
The records of commanderies and states,
and the books of genealogies,
strive to boast of their regions,
and flaunt their clans.
How can readers not examine their merits and faults,
and distinguish their truth and falsehood?
As for the "Five Talents of Jiāngdōng,"
they originated from the *Records of Kuàijī*,
and the "Eight Dragons of Yǐngchuān,"
came from the *Xún Family Biography*,
yet those who compiled the histories of Hàn and Jìn
all adopted these empty praises,
and confirmed them as truthful records.
If they are not scrutinized,
how can their right and wrong be detailed?
The School of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
its origins trace back to the Three Dynasties.
According to the Jí Zhǒng Suǒ Yǔ, events from the time of Tài Dīng
were recorded in the Xià and Yīn Spring and Autumn Annals.
Confucius said:
"To be broad in knowledge and understand distant matters
is the teaching of the Shū."
"To compile phrases and compare events
is the teaching of the Spring and Autumn Annals."
Thus, we know the Spring and Autumn Annals began to be composed
around the same time as the Shàng Shū.
The Suǒ Yǔ also mentions the Jìn Spring and Autumn Annals,
recording events from the seventeenth year of Duke Xiàn.
The Guó Yǔ states:
Jìn's Yáng Shé Xī was well-versed in the Spring and Autumn Annals,
and Duke Dào had him instruct his crown prince.
In the Zuǒ Zhuàn, the second year of Duke Zhāo,
Jìn's Hán Xuānzǐ came on a diplomatic mission
and saw the Lǔ Spring and Autumn Annals, saying:
"The rites of Zhōu are fully preserved in Lǔ."
This shows that the title "Spring and Autumn Annals"
was not exclusive to one school.
As for those that have been lost and forgotten,
they are too numerous to record.
Furthermore, according to the Zhú Shū Jì Nián,
its recorded events are identical to those in the Lǔ Spring and Autumn Annals.
Mencius said:
"In Jìn, it is called Shèng,
in Chǔ, it is called Táowù,
and in Lǔ, it is called Spring and Autumn Annals,
but their essence is the same."
Thus, Shèng, Jì Nián, and Táowù
are all alternative names for the Spring and Autumn Annals!
Therefore, Mòzǐ said:
"I have seen the Spring and Autumn Annals of a hundred states,"
referring precisely to this.
In human life,
there are both the virtuous and the unworthy.
If one's vices can serve as warnings to the world,
and one's virtues can serve as examples for posterity,
yet upon death their names remain unheard of,
whose fault is this?
It is the responsibility of the historian.
When the Jin dynasty received the Mandate of Heaven,
the entire realm was unified.
The writer Chén Shòu
then compiled the history of the Three Kingdoms.
Previously, only the histories of two kingdoms had been recorded,
but here it is called the Three Kingdoms
based on the work compiled by Chén Shòu.
He authored the Records of the Three Kingdoms,
comprising sixty-five chapters in total.
At that time, Xiàhóu Zhàn was also writing the Book of Wei,
but upon seeing Chén Shòu's work,
he destroyed his own draft and ceased writing.
After Chén Shòu passed away,
Fàn Jū, the Grand Impartial in Liángzhōu, submitted a memorial stating that the Records of the Three Kingdoms clearly illustrated successes and failures,
its language full of exhortations and warnings,
beneficial for moral transformation,
and he hoped it would be accepted and preserved.
Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued to the Governor of Hénán,
to go to Chén Shòu's home and transcribe his book.
The case of Sui's establishment involved the killing of Zichǐ,
which occurred in the final years of Duke Wén.
It is said to be in the late years of Duke Xī,
but the actual era—"actual era," also written as "chronological era"—differs greatly.
How can the account be so contradictory?
Preface by Huáng Shūlín of Běipíng.
Up until the time of Fàn Yè, Governor of Xuānchéng in the Sòng dynasty,
he extensively gathered scholars,
exhaustively studied ancient texts,
removed redundancies and filled in omissions,
composing the Book of the Later Hàn,
which consisted of ten annals, ten treatises, and eighty biographies,
totaling one hundred chapters.
However, Fàn Yè was arrested for a crime,
and his ten treatises remained unfinished at his death.
On the right, seventy-five characters are removed,
and ten characters are added.
According to the text, only eight characters are actually added.
Generally, authors
before the Wei dynasty
mostly emulated the Three Histories;
from the Jin dynasty onward,
they preferred to study the Five Classics.
The literary style of histories is shallow and easy to imitate,
while the meaning of the classics is profound and difficult to emulate;
since the difficulty and ease differ,
the successes and failures also vary.
Those who appear different but share the same spirit
represent the highest form of imitation;
those who appear similar but differ in spirit
represent the lowest form of imitation.
Yet people all prefer similarity in appearance with difference in spirit,
and do not esteem difference in appearance with similarity in spirit.
Why is this?
It is because their discernment is unclear,
and their preferences are often biased,
delighting in what resembles history but disliking true history.
This is why Zǐzhāng criticized the state of Lǔ,
and there is the allegory of Lord Yè's fondness for dragons.
Yuán Shānsōng said:
"There are five difficulties in writing:
being verbose and disorganized,
is the first difficulty;
being vulgar and lacking classical elegance,
is the second difficulty;
failing to record the truth,
rewarding and punishing inappropriately,
is the fourth difficulty;
and the literary form not matching the substance,
is the fifth difficulty."
To imitate the ancients and yet not resemble them
is the utmost difficulty—
why did he omit this point?
Alas!
Since the time of Sīmǎ Qiān,
it seems none have recognized this principle.
May the enlightened of later generations
take this as a warning!
In examining Sīmǎ Qiān's Records of the Grand Historian,
which begins from the era of Xuānyuán (Yellow Emperor)
and extends down to the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
the territorial scope is vast,
and the historical trajectory is long.
Therefore, his autobiographical account starts with his clan's origin from Zhònglí,
and ends with his own position as Grand Historian.
Although it ranges widely across time,
it never goes beyond the timeframe covered in Records of the Grand Historian.
As for Bān Gù's Book of Hàn,
it only narrates events of the two hundred years of the Western Hàn capital.
Yet his autobiographical section
traces back to the office of Lìngyǐn,
beginning from the time of King Wén of Chǔ;
and includes his work "Response to a Guest's Jest,"
dating to the reign of Emperor Míng of Hàn.
The range it encompasses
far exceeds that of the main text.
Later autobiographical accounts,
produced by more than one author,
all strove to emulate Bān Gù (Mèngjiān),
following this trend without restraint.
When applied to family records,
this approach might still be acceptable;
but when included in state histories,
its flaws become evident.
The Zuǒshì Zhuàn records that during the time of Duke Xiāng of Lǔ,
in Sòng, a girl was born red and hairy,
and abandoned beneath an embankment.
The attendant of Duchess Gòng Jī, mother of Duke Píng of Sòng, saw and rescued her,
thus naming her Qì (Abandoned).
When she grew up, she was beautiful,
and was taken by Duke Píng,
bearing a son named Zuǒ.
Later, the Sòng minister Yī Lì
slandered the crown prince Cuó,
leading to his death.
Original note:
This event occurred in the 26th year of Duke Xiāng.
Before this,
the senior official Huà Yuán had fled to Jìn,
【Original note:
This event occurred in the 15th year of Duke Chéng】,
and Huà Hé Bǐ fled to Wèi.
【Original note:
This event occurred in the 6th year of Duke Zhāo.
】Liú Xiàng seemed to regard this as a clear response to the calamity of fire and red portents at that time.
I note that the occurrence of calamities and auspicious signs
is meant to correspond to later events;
the manifestation of events
should align with prior omens.
For instance, Huà Yuán's flight to Jìn
occurred in the 15th year of Duke Chéng,
yet correlating it with the abandonment at the embankment
is difficult to reconcile.
Moreover, Hé Bǐ's flight to Wèi
occurred in the 6th year of Duke Zhāo,
yet it is grouped with Yuán's flight
(also recorded as "Huà Yuán fled to Jìn")
under the same "before this."
Thus, the sequence of earlier and later events
is contradictory in these accounts.
Inner Chapters Volume Ten
Thus examining these five faults,
to seek the meaning in the texts,
though matters may appear similar in form,
the words are inevitably based on falsehoods.
For carving ice into jade discs,
cannot yield anything usable;
drawing cakes on the ground,
cannot provide anything edible.
Therefore when practiced in the world,
both superiors and inferiors deceive each other;
when transmitted to later generations,
it shows people nothing credible.
Yet the writers of our time,
constantly fail to examine this,
gathering those empty theories,
compiling and arranging them,
beginning from daily records,
culminating in national histories,
connecting chapters and recording extensively,
not omitting a single word,
they cease to be historical works,
but rather become literary collections.
From this point onward,
many followed Fàn Yè's example.
Wèi Shōu inherited this practice,
and carried it to even greater extremes.
When compiling the history of Wèi, he included neighboring states of the Wèi period,
and above the names of their rulers,
he added their territorial designations,
and further specified their official titles.
Thus, for instance, the emperors of Jiāngdōng
were labeled "Usurper of Jìn, Sīmǎ Ruì" and "Island Barbarian Liú Yù";
while the tribal chiefs of Héxī
were called "Self-appointed Governor of Liángzhōu, Zhāng Shí" and "Self-appointed King of Liáng, Lǐ Gǎo."
These designations were not only included within the chapters,
but also listed in full at the beginning of each volume.
Had it been according to Wèi Shōu's intent,
and had he been the one to compile the two Hàn Histories and the Records of the Three Kingdoms,
when entitling the biographies of rebels and bandits,
he would surely have written "Usurper King of Western Chǔ, Xiàng Yǔ" and "Illegitimate King Ningshuò, Wéi Xiāo."
As for the rest—such as Chén Shè, Zhāng Bù, Liú Zhāng, Yuán Shù—
he would have meticulously listed each of their titles and ranks,
leaving nothing unmentioned.
Observing Liú Xiàng's response to Emperor Chéng,
he discussed the deeds of Emperors Wǔ and Xuān,
noting that the traditions passed down were inaccurate,
as detailed in the *Fēngsú Tōng*,
his words can be considered a clear mirror.
Yet when he himself composed the *Hóng Fàn*, *Wǔ Xíng*,
and the biographies in *Xīn Xù*, *Shuō Yuàn*, *Liè Nǚ*, and *Shén Xiān*,
he extensively recounted fictional events,
and fabricated many false statements.
It was not that his knowledge was insufficient or his talent lacking,
but rather because the world is full of people who can be deceived.
Alas!
The younger generation is to be feared,
for there is no era without talented individuals,
so how could one be so careless and dismissive!
That hearsay distorts the truth,
and recording events inaccurately,
is often unavoidable,
something no one can entirely escape.
But to deliberately create strange theories,
to mislead future generations,
is an even greater fault!
The old edition ends the section here,
which is incorrect.
Consider Sū Qín's reply to King Yì of Yān,
where he mentioned a woman who intended to kill her husband,
ordering his concubine to serve him poisoned wine,
but the concubine pretended to stumble and spilled it.
Also, Gān Mào said to Sū Dài (or mistakenly written as "Shì"):
A poor man's daughter and a rich man's daughter were spinning together, and she said:
"I have no means to buy candles,
yet your light is abundant;
you could share your surplus light with me,
without diminishing your own brightness."
The character "exile,"
in the historical text is written as "then with"
two characters.
Master Jiǎ was appointed as the Grand Tutor to the King of Chángshā.
After Master Jiǎ bid farewell and departed,
the historical text includes the character "travel."
Hearing that Chángshā was low-lying and damp,
he personally believed the historical text lacked the character "for."
He thought his lifespan would not be long.
Moreover, he was exiled and leaving,
his heart was discontent.
Upon crossing the Xiāng River,
he composed a rhapsody to mourn Qū Yuán,
the words of which read as follows, and so on.
Shǔ was initially named Chéng,
later renamed Hàn.
Lǐ Shì's Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Cháng Qú compiled the Hàn Shū in ten volumes.
Later it entered the Jìn dynasty's secret archives,
and was renamed Shǔ Lǐ (missing the character "Lǐ")
Shū.
Qú also compiled the Huáyáng Guó Zhì,
which fully records the rise and fall of the Lǐ family.
The people of Chǔ called the owl "jiū".
Since Master Jiǎ was relegated to reside in Chángshā,

his lifespan would not be long,

Thus, although Wáng Píng recognized characters,
he only knew ten;
and though Huò Guāng lacked learning,
he was ignorant of even one classic.
Yet when recounting their words,
they invariably cited canonical texts.
Moreover, Jiāng Chōng and Xīfū Gōng slandered and deluded the emperor,
causing disaster to extend to the crown prince,
and poison to reach loyal and virtuous officials.
In assessing their treacherous villainy,
they far surpassed Shí Xiǎn.
Yet Bān Gù narrated their stories,
without placing them among the sycophants.
Yáng Wángsūn's naked burial violated ritual,
making him a reckless and unrestrained individual;
examining his entire life,
he had no other notable deeds,
yet he was grouped together with Zhū Yún in one biography—there is a character "réng".
and placed at the head of the collected biographies,
is this not defiling?

one character is left blank.
They were also brilliant and illustrious,
yet loyal officials and righteous scholars had not compiled or recorded them.
Therefore, the court again ordered the Palace Attendant and Chief of Reception Liú Zhēn and the Grand Master of Remonstrance Lǐ Yóu (some texts erroneously write "Chōng"),
to variously compose records and tables,
including biographies of famous officials, principled scholars, Confucian scholars, and maternal relatives,
beginning from the Jiànwǔ era
(Emperor Guāngwǔ's reign),
and ending with the Yǒngchū era
(Emperor Ān's reign).
The work was nearly completed when Liú Zhēn and Lǐ Yóu (some texts write "et al.")
passed away successively.

The court then again ordered the Palace Attendant Fú Wújì and the Grand Master of Remonstrance Huáng Jǐng to compose tables for various kings, princes, meritorious officials, and marquises of imperial favor,
biographies of the Southern Chányú and Western Qiāng,
and the Treatise on Geography.
But since the world began to value literary embellishment,
and the masters of poetry championed ornate excess,
then Jùsòng lost his way,
while Língjūn took the helm.
Whenever there was a "worthy" character,
the Western Bureau had empty posts,
the Eastern Library awaited talent,
and all appointments made
were inevitably given to literary scholars.
Thus, those holding brushes and carrying inkstones
mostly lacked the discernment for evaluation and synthesis;
piling chapter upon chapter and document upon document,
they rarely encountered subtle and refined words.
Yet the entire common practice considered this the capable affair,
and at that time, no one dared to disrespect it.
Suppose there were among them
those with methods like Biāo and Qiáo,
talents such as Bān and Xún,
possessing the insight of unique understanding,
and bearing the work of enduring value,
yet all found themselves constrained by prevailing customs,
and ridiculed by cliques.
Thereupon, they ended up eating dregs and drinking thin wine,
bowing to follow reckless creations,
clad in coarse clothes yet harboring jade within,
with no means to present themselves.
This is what Guǎn Zhòng called "employing noble men but mixing in petty men,
the way to harm hegemony."
Yet critics casually ridicule the records of Shěn Yuē and Xiāo Zǐxiǎn in the *Book of Song* and *Book of Southern Qí*,
claiming their accounts are twice as lengthy as those of Sǔn Shèng and Xí Yàozhī;
who both wrote histories of Jìn. Huà Qiáo and Xiè Chén’s compilations are both *Books of Later Hàn*.
Their language is more verbose than that of Bān Gù and Sīmǎ Qiān—these four lines were disordered and incoherent in the old text, recorded later in the chapter.
Is this not absurd!
Hence it is said:
"When discussing the brevity or verbosity of historical writings,
one should only examine whether events are inaccurately recorded,
or words are omitted where they should be written.
That is what matters.
To necessarily measure the thickness or thinness of worldly affairs,
and limit the number of chapters and sections,
is unreasonable."
This saying refers to exactly that.
The Basic Annals of the Records of the Grand Historian states:
Gǔsǒu had Shùn dig a well,
who secretly made a side tunnel to escape.
Gǔsǒu and Xiàng together filled the well with earth.
The Book of Han records that Chéng Fāngsuì falsely claimed to be the exiled crown prince,
arriving at the palace gate.
Juàn Bùyí said:
"In the past, Wèi Kuǎiguì offended his late father,
and when he sought to enter the state,
Crown Prince Zhé refused to admit him."
This wording slightly differs from that in the Book of Han.
The Spring and Autumn Annals approved of this.
Thereupon, he ordered his arrest and handed him over to the officials.
Huò Guāng thus began to value Confucian learning.
Examining the quotation by Juàn,
it is the main text of the Gongyang Commentary.
As in the Analects, Rǎn Yǒu asked:
"Is our Master in favor of the ruler of Wèi?"
Zǐgòng replied:
"Our Master is not in favor of it."
Why so?
Because father and son were contending for the state,
like the spring gibbon serving Cáo,
it was intolerable by ritual and law,
and detested by moral teachings.
Yet the Gongyang Commentary interprets the meaning,
instead considering Wèi Zhé to be virtuous,
which violates the Master's teaching,
loses the sage's intent,
encourages evil followers,
and misleads later learners.
This is its fifth shortcoming.
If we compare its three strengths
with these five shortcomings,
the principle of victory or defeat,

can be decisively known.
However, since the capitals of Xiányáng and Luòyáng were no longer held,
the imperial throne moved south,
the region east of the Yangtze River became the land of rites and music,
and Jīnlíng truly served as the repository of texts and records.
Thus, its customs still preserved speech that adhered to norms and restraints,
and words that delighted in elegance and refinement.
Even in moments of turmoil and haste,

they did not forget the classics, as seen in the History of Liáng, which records Emperor Gāozǔ, while besieged, saying to Xiāo Zhèngdé: "They sob and weep, but what use is lamenting now?" And when Prince Xiāngdōng heard that his eldest son, Fāngděng, had been killed, he said to his second son, Fāngzhū: "If it were not for the downfall, how could you, my lord, rise?" These are examples of such speech.
Moreover, the official historians polished the records,
without expending excessive effort.
The way of historiography
has two streams.
What are they?
Recording events and speeches
originates from the documents of that time;
compiling and editing
belongs to the brush of later generations.
Now, those who draft initially
rely on broad knowledge and faithful records,
like Dǒng Hú and Nánshǐ.
Those who systematize later
value keen insight and comprehensive talent,
like Bān Gù and Chén Shòu.
If we must discuss their tasks,
they differ in sequence.
Yet they depend on each other to achieve completion,
and their goal is the same principle.
Original pronunciation: shǐ (上声).
You and Ying produce extraordinary scholars,
the Yangtze and Han rivers nurture heroic spirits,
where remarkable figures are born,
bringing glory to their commanderies and states.
Therefore, local scholars
compile and record their stories.
Such as Quān Chēng's Elder Figures of Chénliú, Zhōu Fěi (also written as "Zhōu Péi")
with Former Worthies of Rǔnán, Chén Shòu's Elder Figures of Yì Province, and Yú Yù's Historical Records of Kuàijī.
These are what we call "commandery records."
In the tenth year of Duke Yin, in winter,
there was a heavy hailstorm.
The current Records writes "snow,"
suspected that the early Tang version had "hail."
It then records Liú Xiàng's prognostication,
followed by stating the Gongyang Classic says "heavy hailstorm,"
and continues with Dǒng Shēng's explanation.
Observing the Liang and Tang dynasties,
they compiled the histories of Qi and Sui.
While Emperor Donghun was still alive,
they hastily listed the He era;
before Emperor Yang had ended,
they had already compiled the "Annals of Gong."
Examining their intentions,

Generally, partial records and minor chronicles
all document events of their immediate time,
and when sought in state histories,
they are considered the most truthful records.
However, their language is often crude and plain,
and events are rarely complete,
ultimately failing to achieve imperishable status,
or eternal transmission to future generations,
serving only as draft material for later writers.
As for anecdotes,
they consist of what previous histories omitted,
recorded by later people;
seeking diverse accounts
can indeed be beneficial.
But when fabricated by the reckless,
they indiscriminately record hearsay
without any selection.
Thus truth and falsehood become indistinguishable,
and right and wrong intermingle in confusion.
For example, Guō Zǐhéng's "Records of the Immortals"
and Wáng Zǐnián's "Collection of Omissions"
are entirely constructed with fictional tales,
used to astonish the ignorant masses.
This represents their most severe flaw.
As for trivial sayings,
they mostly record contemporary debates
and vulgar jokes.
They provide the shrewd with material for wit,
and conversationalists with topics for discussion.
But when handled by the undiscerning,
they contain mutual slander and ridicule,
applied even to ancestors,
with vulgar and indecent words
originating from bedrooms,
all elevated to recorded status,
used as elegant speech,
ultimately offering no benefit to moral standards
while damaging ethical teachings.
As for local histories,
they boast of local worthies,
praising their regional clans;
within their own regions,
they gain considerable circulation;
but when placed elsewhere,
they rarely receive appreciation.
Those like Cháng Qú's meticulous thoroughness
or Liú Bǐng's comprehensive breadth
(some write "Bǐng" incorrectly)
that can achieve immortal transmission
and earn praise from descendants
are indeed few.
As for family histories,
they concern only three clans,
their accounts limited to single households,
suitable only for domestic circulation,
difficult to spread throughout the nation.
Moreover, if family traditions continue unbroken,
their records may still survive
(some write "suī" incorrectly);
but if the lineage perishes,
these writings are lost as well.
As for separate biographies,
they seldom originate from personal insight,
nor from independent thought,
merely compiling previous histories
into collected volumes.
Those containing sufficient novel perspectives
with additional interpretations
amount to barely one-tenth.
For those with limited learning,
they are deeply admired;
but for scholars seeking profundity,
they offer little substance.
As for miscellaneous records,
when discussing immortal paths,
they mention elixirs and breath cultivation
for prolonging life;
when speaking of supernatural realms,
they describe virtue rewarded and vice punished
to discourage evil and encourage good—
this is acceptable.
But when distorted by the erroneous,
they recklessly discuss strange phenomena,
diligently narrating demonic matters,
seeking broad benefit
while offering no valuable meaning.
As for geographical writings,
like those compiled by Zhū Gàn
covering the nine provinces,
or those written by Kàn Yǎn
exhausting the four regions,
their language is elegant and proper,
with unbiased accounts.
Those differing from this

families regarding their cities as famous capitals,
competing to praise their dwellings,
exaggerating beyond reality.
Furthermore, ancient city walls
and famous mountains and rivers

how vulgar!
As for capital city records,
like palaces (some write "inner chambers"),
imperial tombs, streets, and outer walls,

this is acceptable.
But when handled by fools,
they become tedious and excessive,
broad without limits

It is argued:
That which is obscure and unfathomable,
constantly changing without constancy,
cannot be harmed by weapons of war,
nor restrained by nets and snares,
such as Zuǒ Cí transforming his substance into a sheep,
or Liú Gēn slipping into a wall by altering his form.
When the time cannot be shifted,
calamity is certain to arrive—
it must come,
and even the great sages cannot avoid it,
such as when Jī Bó was confined in Yǒulǐ,
or when Kǒng Fù was distressed in Chén and Cài.
Yet foolish people in the world
all say that those who perform such transformations
are the sages.
How could they know that the sages' wisdom encompasses all things,
and their talents combine a hundred virtues?
If it were only like this,
what difference would there be
between them and ordinary men within the bounds of convention?

Yet those who carried out these deeds falsified the facts,

Thus, blame was incurred at the moment,

The narratives in historical records

When there are principles that are hard to rely on

when the Dai state initially relocated,
they modeled after Wu's capital to set up court gates.

the merit of divination and measurement,
which remain unchanged through hundreds of rulers,
and cannot be abandoned for a single day.

Is it not mistaken
to be as inflexible as gluing pegs while tuning a lute?
However, Bān Gù's inconsistencies and contradictions,
being past, cannot be remonstrated,
yet later authors
all follow this confusion.
The Sòngshǐ includes the Wèi dynasty above,
the Suíshū encompasses the Liáng dynasty before.
Seeking the events they record,
one obtains but a fraction.
Once established as precedent,
none dare change it;
contemplating this principle forever,
one can only sigh in regret!
Ten Miscellaneous Notes: Since ancient times, the character "之" has long existed.
Scholars,
in their discussions, are also referred to as "lecturers."
They are numerous.
Those well-versed in the *Gongyang Commentary*
particularly despise the *Zuo Commentary*;
those familiar with the Grand Historian
often add the character "則."
They are biased and envious of Mèng Jiān.
If one can use the strengths of others to attack their weaknesses,
and uphold what is right here to critique what is wrong there,
few are capable of excelling in both.
Some editions end the note here.
Others omit the character "又."
Observing the scholars of the world,
some immerse themselves in a single classic,
while others specialize in one history.
Those discussing the *Spring and Autumn Annals*
do not realize that after the decline of the Zhou dynasty,
six powerful states emerged;
those debating the *Records of the Grand Historian* and the *Book of Han*
fail to grasp that after the fall of the Liú clan,
the land was divided into three kingdoms.
It is like the hermit of Wǔlíng,
who vanished—or "retreated"—
into the traces of Táohuāyuán,
living in the Jin era,
yet still referring to the land as that of the tyrannical Qin.
Even if one's learning spans a thousand years,
and one's books fill five carts,
if upon encountering excellence and integrity one fails to recognize their virtue,
or upon facing contradictions remains unaware of the errors,
then, as Gě Hóng said, they are merely boxes for storing books,
masters of the *Five Classics* in name only.
And as the Master said:
"What is the use of much learning?"
This is precisely what is meant.
Some editions mistakenly combine this with the following note.
Volume Fifteen
Xià Hèlián Bóbó,
Tiānshuǐ Zhào Sīqún, Běidì Zhāng Yuān,
at Zhēnxīng and Bóbó's era.
Chéngguāng Chāngyuán.
One version lacks the character "zhī". Generation,
all were commissioned to compile their state histories.
Until the fall of Tǒngwàn Xià city.
Its demise,
most were burned.
One version omits the character "shāo".
Although Shèng Gōng was of humble origin,
he was already able to gather followers to avenge wrongs,
take refuge among the Greenwoods,
and earn the name of a hero.
How could it be that when he became honored as a ruler,
he instead ended up in such a state?
This is likely the author's biased writing to flatter the times,
solely to embellish Emperor Guāngwǔ's virtues;
using flattering words to please the sovereign,
thereby venting the resentment against Bó Shēng.
Moreover, the history of the restoration
originated from the Eastern Lodge,
perhaps determined by Emperor Míng himself,
or edited by Empress Mǎ;
and as the Han dynasty's fortune was long-lasting,
the official records remained unaltered,
thus allowing later generations to compile retrospectively,
only spreading false accounts.
In Chén Shòu's "Records of the Three Kingdoms,
Biography of the Later Sovereign of Shǔ," it states:
"Shǔ had no official historian,
hence omens and auspicious signs were not recorded."
However, consider the yellow vapor seen in Zìguī,
and the flocks of birds falling into the Jiāng River;
Chéngdū reported the appearance of a propitious star,
while Yìzhōu claimed there was no ministerial aura;
if no historian was appointed,
how were these events recorded?
It is probably because his father suffered the humiliation of head-shaving,
that he thus added these slanderous remarks.
You must think that the various worthies are not adept at editing and compiling,
and because I am straightforward and resolute,
you therefore recommend me as the foremost candidate.
Even if we follow this reasoning,
there is indeed some basis for it.
Why do I say so?
I began serving in office from a young age,
and early on stepped into prominent positions.
When His Majesty first ruled over all states,
and had not yet personally attended to governmental affairs,
due to my maintaining this integrity,
and not associating with treacherous individuals,
I consequently became like an earthen ox in office,
discarded like a straw dog.
Later, when the imperial carriage journeyed west,
with all officials following in full attendance,
I considered that my official duties were simple,
and requested to remain behind.
Residing at the censorate, I often thought the court was unaware of me,
and that the state had finished with me.
How could I have expected that one day I would suddenly receive an imperial decree,
with provincial officials at my door,
and envoys arriving in continuous streams?
Subsequently, I was hastened by four-horse carriage into Hánguān Pass,
passed through countless gates to have an audience with the Son of Heaven.
Summoning Jiǎ Yí to the Xuān Room,
though his talent was admired;
calling Jì Bù from Hédōng,
only increased his shame instead.
Since you, Honorable Sir, hold the position of chief minister,
(the original pronunciation is in the third tone.)
Volume Twelve
The objection states:
A person should only receive a posthumous name
after passing away.
Tián Cháng was still alive,
yet was hastily referred to by his posthumous name—
this inaccuracy
is clearly evident.
Thus it is known.
Furthermore, examining the *Zuǒzhuàn*,
Shí Què said:
"Chén Huángōng was currently favored by the king."
In the *Analects*,
Chén Sībài asked Confucius:
"Does Zhāogōng understand ritual?"
This aligns with the text of the *Records of the Grand Historian*.
In the *Records of the Grand Historian*,
the household steward said to the Grand Emperor:
"Although Gāozǔ is your son,
he is the sovereign."
All such expressions
follow the same pattern.
However, these instances stem from errors
that can be easily corrected through editing.
But the discussion of Chéngzǐ in the "Hereditary House of the Tián Clan"
concludes with rhymed verse,
compiled into song lyrics—
attempting to make corrections
would allow no revision.
Therefore, I single out this error
to serve as a prominent example.
Further, according to the "Odes of Bèi·
Jìng Nǚ"
in the Book of Songs, chapter three,
the gentleman takes her vermilion tube.
Now, the vermilion tube
is what the female historian holds for recording admonitions and instructions.
In ancient times, for rulers,
there were state historians at the outer court,
and female historians at the inner court;
the inner and the outer
shared the same responsibilities.
Thus, when Duke Xiàn of Jìn was deluded and disorderly,
and Lí Jī wept at night,
the intimacies of the bedchamber
and affairs of the private quarters
could not be concealed.
When King Zhāo of Chǔ feasted and roamed,
Jī of Cài responded with her wish,
and the king turned to the historian, saying:
"Write it down;
these twelve characters are missing in the old text,
which must be an omission.
Without these twelve words, it does not form a complete statement.
Jī of Cài has promised to follow me in death."
Thus, even private feasts had records of events,
likely those tasked with such duties were akin to female historians.
By the time of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
there existed the "Private Palace Diary";
Empress Mǎ, known for her illustrious virtue, compiled the "Annals of Emperor Míng’s Reign."
All such writings
seem to have originated from the palace,
yet upon inquiring about their official positions,
no titles or ranks are known.
In the Suí dynasty, Wáng Shào submitted a memorial,
requesting to follow ancient practices,
reestablish the ranks of female historians,
fully record inner court rituals,
and submit them to the outer ministries.
The duties of palace attendants and female historians in the Rites of Zhōu
were managed under the Ministry of Heaven.
This memorial still preserved this intent.
Emperor Wén did not approve,
and thus it was not implemented.
Outer Chapters: Scroll Eighteen
Volume One
The Analects says:
"Tàibó may be called a man of supreme virtue.
Thrice he declined the empire,
and the people could find no words to praise him."
Now, the title Lǚshì Chūnqiū is probably mistaken,
and should be Wú Yuè Chūnqiū.
According to what is recorded,
this was because King Tàiwáng doted on his grandson,
and intended to establish his father.
Tàibó, being the eldest legitimate son,
was indeed in a position that obstructed the worthy.
Had he shamelessly clung to his post,
and harbored doubts without leaving,
at worst he would have faced execution like Jí of Wèi,
at best exile like the crown prince of Chǔ.
Even if he wished not to yield,
could the ruler and father have established him?
Moreover, when King Tàiwáng died,
Tàibó came to mourn,
and Jìlì, following their father's dying command,
yielded to his elder brother.
Tàibó, having already mutilated his body,
was excused with a plea.
The reason he damaged this jade-like body,
and adopted disheveled hair,
was fundamentally to externally eliminate suspicion,
and internally dispel (some texts read 'cherish')
jealousy and mistrust,
like a rooster severing its own tail,
thereby avoiding being used as a human sacrifice.
Also, according to the Spring and Autumn Annals,
Jìn shì (some texts omit 'shì')
Shēnshēng, when about to be deposed, said:
"To be like Wú Tàibó
would still leave a good name."
This shows that Tàibó and Shēnshēng
faced similar situations.
But because their choices differed,
their outcomes were different.
If the Master's judgment of Tàibó
must praise him for turning sickness into beauty,
transforming disaster into blessing,
that would be appropriate.
But to say he "may be called a man of supreme virtue"
is that not erroneously bestowing undue praise?
This is the ninth doubt.
When Fǎ Shèng's book recorded the restoration of the Jin dynasty,
he changed the tables into annotations;
though the naming was clever,
it also contained much redundancy.
At the time when the Jin house was displaced,
holding the south in Yang and Yuè,
and the Wei clan rose abruptly,
dominating the north in Yān and Dài,
among these various usurpers,
there were sixteen houses,
not adhering to the legitimate calendar,
each establishing their own rulers.
Cuī Hóng, in composing his tables,
made considerable clarifications;
compared with the various chapters of the Records of the Grand Historian and the Book of Han,
his work is among the most essential.
It is said:
"By the shores of Pénglí Lake,
fish are used to feed the great."
This indicates what the land is rich in,
does not mean the thing is considered precious.
Now, Qí lies close to the sea,
where scaled and shelled creatures abound,
so high-ranking guests eat meat,
middle-ranking guests eat fish,
omitting "meat-eating middle guests"
four characters.
This was the old custom of Qí.
Yet eating bream and carp,
which poets valued,
when served in other states,
is called a delicacy.
As the Gōngyáng Commentary states:
Duke Líng of Jìn sent a warrior to kill Zhào Dùn,
who saw him eating a fish meal. He said:
"You are a high minister of Jìn yet eat fish meals,
this shows your frugality.
I cannot bear to kill you."
Now, Master Gōngyáng came from the state of Qí,
and was unfamiliar with Jìn's customs,
taking what was common in the eastern land,
to be the same in the western state.
Thus he regarded that fine food,
as plain fare,
recording it in truthful accounts,
making it a maxim.
Not only does this contradict the Zuǒ Commentary,
but it completely misses the reality of things.
According to the Records of the Grand Historian, prior to the Spring and Autumn period,
all records of state calamities and anomalies,
as well as the prognostications of sages and wise men,
are derived from the Zuo Zhuan and the Discourses of the States.
The citations in the current Treatise of the Han,
range from the reigns of Kings Yōu and Lì of the Zhou dynasty above,
to those of Dukes Dìng and Āi of the state of Lǔ below.
In the pre-Qin era before the Warring States period,
all writings could be chanted and recited,
not merely due to editorial polishing,
but truly because their inherent quality was naturally excellent.
How can this be verified?
Take for instance "鹑贲"
"鸲鹆",
which were children's rhymes;
"山木"
"辅车",
which were contemporary proverbs;
"皤腹弃甲",
the songs of city defenders;
"原田是谋",
the chants of carriage riders.
Though these were all crude words and humble phrases,
they still maintained such warmth and refinement,
let alone the scholars who stood girdled at court,
further endowed with extensive knowledge and ancient wisdom!
Thus we understand that when contemporaries spoke,
and historians recorded their words,
though there might be deliberation and polishing,
the essence never lost its fundamental character.
People's understanding may be penetrating or obstructed,
their spirit may be clear or obscured.
Thus censure and praise differ accordingly,
and love and hatred vary individually.
When the Three Sovereigns suffered slander,
they encountered Lǔ Lián and gained vindication;
when the Five Hegemons monopolized fame,
they met Kǒng Xuān and were disparaged.
This shows that while things possess constant standards,
appraisal lacks fixed criteria.
To seek balanced and accurate judgment,
is this not a once-in-a-millennium encounter?
Moreover, historical texts as writings
are profound and vast (some editions read "source-like"),
broad and extensive.
If scholars cannot explore the profound and seek the hidden,
reach the distant and plumb the depths,
how (some editions read "then")
can they sufficiently distinguish their advantages and disadvantages,
and clarify their good and evil?
Street talk and alley gossip,
often contain noteworthy insights;
minor tales and trivial sayings
are still better than nothing at all.
Thus, gentlemen with a taste for such matters
do not discard any of them.
Works like Liú Yìqìng's *Shì Shuō*, Péi Róngqī's *Yǔ Lín*, Kǒng Sīshàng's *Yǔ Lù*, and Yáng Jièsōng's (or "Sōngjiè")

Volume Six
The records in the "Basic Annals" are made clear
through the biographies;
tables and treatises are of different forms,
and need not be interrelated.
In older histories, the volumes of tables and treatises were placed between the basic annals and biographies,
but when it came to Fàn Yè,
he initiated reforms,
which Shěn Yuē and Wèi Shōu followed in their works,
adhering to this practice.
Later, Xiāo Zǐxiǎn in his "Book of Southern Qí" and Kǒng Yǐngdá in his "History of Suì"
did not follow this model,
but instead returned to Bān Gù's method.
For one should choose what is good and act accordingly,
regardless of its origin in time or place;
my concern is
to hear of what is right and not move toward it.
To deliberate comprehensively,
those compiled by years and months are called annals,
and those arranged with annals and biographies are called records,
which follow the chronological order,
this being the most excellent method.
Now names are meant to define forms,
serving as subsidiaries to substance;
if they stray from the proper path,
they violate the fundamental principles.
Consider the works of Lǚ and Văn,
each authoring a book,
merely sequencing chapters and sections,
without connecting them to specific times and months.
These are actually miscellaneous records of philosophical schools,
yet both are titled Spring and Autumn Annals.
Yú Huàn and Yáo Chá composed histories of Wei and Liang,
recording all details great and small,
with excessive trivialities and redundancies,
yet both labeled them as summaries.
Examining their names against their substance,
how greatly do they miss the mark!
Observing the tables created by Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān,
for emperors and kings, he narrates their descendants,
for dukes and marquises, he records their years and months,
arranging rows that intertwine and connect,
compiling characters closely to align with one another.
Though Yān and Yuè are ten thousand lǐ apart,
within the space of an inch,
they can interlock like dog's teeth;
though there are nine generations of ancestral lines,
within a square foot (some texts say "inch"),
they are arranged
in orderly lines like wild geese.
This allows readers
to see clearly upon reading the text,
and understand at a glance,
which is why it is so satisfying.
As for Bān Gù's "Table of Ancient and Modern Persons,"
it solely focuses on evaluating the wise and foolish,
and promoting good and condemning evil.
Since it does not deal with the state's hereditary succession,
or the inheritance of ranks and positions,
yet it still uses multiple rows and boundaries,
narrow writing and small characters,
compared to other tables,
it hardly seems to belong to the same category!
Indeed, listing people from ancient to modern times
fundamentally differs from the purpose of tables,
and if one insists on retaining it,
it should rather be titled as a "record."
Starting from the highest grade
down to the lowest,
each should be clearly marked,
with distinct categories and rules,
organizing by type into chapters,
and ordering by quality as the sequence.
Then, at the end of each chapter, state,
"On the right (some texts omit 'right'),
so many grades,
totaling so many persons."
This is similar to the "Treatise on Geography," which begins by describing the capital,
and ends by detailing the border regions;
first listing the provinces and counties,
then mentioning the population.
After crossing the river, he was appointed as a Gentleman of Writings,
and received an imperial order to compile the history of Jin.
He was accused by his colleague Yǔ Yù,
the old text says "reprimanded," which is incorrect.
He was dismissed from office due to the incident.
His family was poor and lacked resources,
and the book was not yet completed.
He then sought refuge with General of the West-Pacifying Army Yǔ Liàng in Wǔchāng Garrison.
Liàng provided him with paper and brushes,
and thus he was able to complete it,
producing a total of eighty-nine volumes of the Book of Jin.
In the sixth year of the Xiánkāng era,
he finally went to the court to present it.
Although Yǐn was fond of writing,
his style was clumsy and his talent limited.
The well-organized parts of the book
were all revised by Quán;
the sections with chaotic and unclear sentences
were certainly written by Yǐn.
At the time, Gān Bǎo, a Gentleman of the Masters of Writing in charge of the national history,
also compiled the Annals of Jin,
covering seven emperors from Emperor Xuān to Emperor Mǐn,
a span of fifty-three years,
in a total of twenty-two volumes.
His work was concise,
straightforward yet tactful,
and was highly praised at the time.
Generally, since ancient times, the compilation by official historians
has followed this general outline.
For arranging expressions and comparing events,
linking months to years,
forms the foundation of historical writing,
serving as the eyes and ears for living people—
these aspects are largely covered here.
As for the remaining specialized records (some texts erroneously write "compiled")
and minor accounts or fiction,
there is no time to discuss them in detail.
When warfare is raging fiercely,
and victory or defeat remains undecided,
there are those who do not adhere to the orthodox calendar,
and establish their own rulers and chieftains.
If the state histories are to record their biographies,
it is appropriate to establish separate categories.
For instance, the various heroes like Chén Shè and Xiàng Yǔ
were included in the records of the Hàn;
the rebels such as Dǒng Zhuó and Yuán Shào
were attached to the "Records of Wèi."
Since they were treated under the same category as subjects,
how can one distinguish the differences between them?
Only the "Dōngguàn" listed figures like the Pínglín and Xiàjiāng groups under "Records of Dependent States."
However, later writers
did not follow this example.
It was not until the "New History of Jìn"
that the sixteen states' rulers were first designated under "Records of Dependent States" in the tables,
which can be said to be choosing the good to practice,
skillfully emulating antiquity.
In the Spring and Autumn Annals, when the heir apparent was in mourning,
if he was deposed before completing a full year,
he was not considered a full-fledged ruler,
and thus no separate chapter was created for him.
Therefore, among the twelve dukes of Lǔ,
È and Shì were not included in their ranks.
As for Zǐyīng of Qín,
and Chāngyì of Hàn,
both were recorded due to Húhài,
and became known by being attached to Emperor Zhāo of Hàn.
Yet Wú Jūn's "Annals of Qí" used Yùlín as a reign title,
failing to follow ancient practices,
how excessively arbitrary this was!
Original note:
Examination of the Bamboo Annals first reached this meaning.
But since ancient times, those who interpreted the Spring and Autumn Annals
all made arbitrary explanations.
For example, when Cáo and Mǎ received the Mandate,
they personally became emperors,
not as feudal lords guarding their domains
while implementing the imperial calendar.
Yet Sūn Shèng's Two Yangqiu on Wèi and Jìn,
whenever recording the beginning of a year,
invariably wrote "In the spring of such year, the Emperor's first month."
Since the year was already compiled according to imperial annals,
and the month was again listed with the emperor's name,
using this to imitate the Spring and Autumn Annals
is what is called similar in appearance but different in essence.
Yet from Yáo's time backward,
the sages and worthies still recorded,
seeking one or two traces,
something vaguely remains.
But later scholars,
widely invented strange tales,
creating accounts predating Táng and Yú.
Their words lack classical basis,
their writings contradict the sages.
Thus Sīmǎ Qiān declared:
"Before Shénnóng's era,
I know nothing."
Bān Gù likewise said:
"Regarding Zhuānxū's affairs,
none can be clearly known."
This shows what the ancient texts record
contains nothing that can be verified.
In the past, Confucius had the strength to lift a city gate bar,
yet he was not renowned for his physical power.
Why is that?

anxiously (older versions read "fearfully") wandering in exile,
was able to trace back to Yáo and Shùn,
and model himself on King Wén and King Wǔ.
Why must one occupy the sovereign's position,
or hold the尊facing-south尊尊,
to be called one who connects categories!
Discussion Four.
What Péi Sōngzhī discusses
is a very trivial matter,
one version reads "lowly."
Moreover, the writing and reasoning are not skillful.
Observing the periods prior to the Zhou and Qin dynasties,
the selection of historians,
its details cannot be heard of.
As for the times from the Han and Wei dynasties onward,
it can be discussed.
However, many falsely held empty titles,
having reputation without substance.
According to Liú's History of the Later Han and Cáo's Records of the Wei,
these two histories,
both compiled in their respective eras,
those who were able to accomplish the task,
were likely only individuals like Liú Zhēn, Cài Yōng, Wáng Chén, and Yú Huàn.
Yet old histories record their collaborative work,
involving not just one school.
For instance, Wáng Yì and Ruǎn Jí also participated among them.
One miswritten as "example."
Moreover, Shūshī delved into the study of chapters and sentences,
a pedantic Confucian scholar;
Sìzōng indulged in the depths of fermented grains,
a wild drunkard.
How could they possibly coordinate—alternatively written as "arrange"—
contemporary affairs,
and formulate the state's statutes?
How strange it was!
When the Jìn dynasty possessed the empire,
after Luòyáng was destroyed and laid waste,
the officials and nobles crossed the river southward,
and in Jiāngzuǒ, prefectures and counties were established for the émigrés,
with no regard for their native places.
Thus, in the region corresponding to the constellations Dǒu and Niú,
there were prefectures called Qīngzhōu and Xúzhōu;
and in the lands of Wú and Yuè,
provinces were designated as Jìzhōu and Yùzhōu.
If one wished to ensure that north and south would not be confused,
and that the waters of Zī and Shéng could be distinguished,
was it possible?
Those who clung to empty names for their native lands
would not change them even after a hundred generations.
As time passed and the world became enduring,
writing and cart tracks were unified.
Prefectures and counties were abolished and established without constancy,
and their names differed between ancient and modern times.
Yet when authors wrote biographies of individuals,
they often stated, "This person was from such-and-such a place,"
using the old designations for the locations,

applying them to recent times. For instance, in writing a biography of someone from the Wáng family in modern history, they would say, "A person from Lángyá, Línyí"; in writing a biography of someone from the Lǐ family, they would say, "A person from Lǒngxī, Chéngjì," and so on. Not only had the Wáng and Lǐ clans long left their original homes, but also, at that time, such prefectures and counties no longer existed; these were all old names from before the Jìn and Wèi dynasties.
If one seeks a true record,
is it not difficult indeed!
The Book of Changes says:
"In ancient times, people knotted ropes to govern,
and later sages replaced them with written contracts."
Some scholars suspect "contracts" should be "commentaries,"
referring to those who annotated the classics.
It is said:
Fúxī shì "first drew the eight trigrams,
created written contracts,
to replace the governance by knotted ropes,
and from then on, written records prevailed."
It is also said:
"The books of Fúxī, Shénnóng, and Huángdì are called the 'Three Fén,'
which speak of the great Way;
the books of Shàohào, Zhuānxū, Gāoxīn, Táng, and Yú are called the 'Five Diǎn,'
which speak of the constant Way."
The Spring and Autumn Annals records that the historian of Chǔ,
likely meaning "Yǐ Xiāng,"
could read the Three Fén and Five Diǎn.
The Book of Rites says:
"The outer historian is in charge of the books of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors."
From this, it can be said
that the meaning of the Fén and Diǎn texts,
the Three and Five historical records,
by the time of the Spring and Autumn period,
were still widely circulated in the world.
However, by later ages,
these books were no longer transmitted.
Only from the time of Táng and Yú onward,
can we speak of what remains.
There are also cases where like attracts like,
as illustrated by past figures.
For instance, Wáng Yǐn claimed that Zhūgě Liàng issued challenges,
hoping to gain advantages like Cáo Jiù;
Cuī Hóng stated that Mùróng Chōng received favor,
due to possessing the charm of Lóng Yáng.
These accounts correspond,
and the words are straightforward indeed.
However, Lú Sīdào claimed that Xíng Shào did not grieve over his son's death,
a phenomenon unseen since Dōngmén Wú;
this had never occurred before;
Lǐ Bǎiyào asserted that Wáng Lín truly won people's hearts,
even Lǐ Jiāngjūn's earnest and persuasive guidance
could not surpass it.
These are but empty references to ancient events,
falsely embellishing mediocre words,
merely flaunting their learning,
and must be discerned as inappropriate.
In the thirty-third year of Duke Xī's reign in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, in the twelfth month,
frost fell but did not kill the grass.
Below this, Liú Xiàng's prognostication connects it to the three families expelling Duke Zhāo.
In the fifth year of Duke Chéng's reign,
Mount Liáng collapsed.
Liú Xiàng's prognostication also relates it to the three families expelling Duke Zhāo of Lǔ.
In the seventh year,
a field mouse gnawed the horns of the sacrificial ox.
According to the "Spring and Autumn Annals with Zuo's Commentary" explaining the "Classic," it states:
When a state is destroyed and its territory is taken,
it is called "entering,"
such as entering Chén,
entering Wèi,
entering Zhèng,
entering Xǔ,
which illustrates this principle.
As for the Battle of Bǎijǔ,
the defeat of Zǐcháng,
on the Gēngchén day, Wú entered,
yet it is uniquely recorded as Yǐng.
Now, the feudal lords held ranks,
and each established their capital cities,
"state" refers to Chǔ,
"capital" refers to Yǐng.
Only the state's name is taken,
not the capital's designation.
Why is it that Yǐng is recorded as entered,
omitting the name Chǔ,
compared to other examples,
how inconsistent it is!
Examining the records in the two commentaries,
referring to the "Classic" recorded in the "Gōngyáng" and "Gǔliáng" commentaries.
Both state "entering Chǔ,"
could it be that the original text of "Zuo's Commentary,"
also referring to the "Classic,"
is uniquely mistaken?
"Mistaken" means in error.
